cards.title: One-Feature Email: Selling Ingredient and Spec Differentiation
cards.summary: Feature a single ingredient, material or spec to distinguish a product that otherwise sounds identical to competitors.
cards.use_when: Writing product emails when every competitor claims the same benefit (e.g. protein powder that all says 'gain muscle').

cards.title: Single-FAQ Email to Kill Objections
cards.summary: Answer one frequently asked customer question per email to overcome objections and quietly position the product.
cards.use_when: Mining support tickets and reviews for purchase objections to turn into campaign content.

cards.title: 'What's Inside' Email for Bundles and Consumables
cards.summary: Unpack everything included with an order in a skimmable list to remove pre-purchase uncertainty.
cards.use_when: Selling bundles, kits or consumable products where buyers don't know exactly what they'll receive.

cards.title: How-It's-Made and How-To-Use Emails
cards.summary: Turn your production process or usage instructions into a story-driven email that signals quality and removes complexity objections.
cards.use_when: Reducing hesitation on a product that seems complicated, or building brand story for a physical product.

cards.title: Back-in-Stock Email Leveraging Popularity and Urgency
cards.summary: Use the back-in-stock angle to combine popularity proof with scarcity, even for products that never truly sold out.
cards.use_when: New inventory arrives, or you want a high-urgency campaign angle on restocked or returned items.

cards.title: Trending Product Email — Frame Future, Not Past
cards.summary: Promote best-performing products by framing them as upcoming trends rather than last season's favorites.
cards.use_when: Highlighting top sellers or building seasonal collection emails on your store.

cards.title: Reviews and Testimonials Email for Social Proof
cards.summary: Feature a small number of customer reviews or social comments to prove legitimacy and trigger herd behavior.
cards.use_when: Building trust for a newer brand or nudging hesitant subscribers with peer proof.

cards.title: Us vs Them Comparison Email
cards.summary: Compare your product against competitors in a clear table to help buyers choose you without begging for the sale.
cards.use_when: Competitive categories where buyers are weighing alternatives before purchase.

cards.title: Myth vs Fact Email
cards.summary: Bust common industry misconceptions to overcome objections with an engaging, curiosity-driven premise.
cards.use_when: Your niche has persistent misinformation (sunscreen, supplements, etc.) that blocks purchases.

cards.title: Blog Promo Email That Sells the Click
cards.summary: Use a sneak peek to drive traffic to a blog post, warming subscribers and enabling soft-sell product placement.
cards.use_when: You have blog content and want engagement that moves people down the funnel without a hard pitch.

cards.title: Research Study Highlight Email
cards.summary: Cite a published study related to your niche to position the brand as an industry leader and lateral proof.
cards.use_when: Looking for high-credibility campaign content that your list rarely sees.

cards.title: Holiday Email Using Obscure Holidays
cards.summary: Anchor fun emails to unusual daily holidays connected to your niche rather than only major holidays.
cards.use_when: Filling campaign calendar gaps and adding engagement without overt promotion.

cards.title: 15 Rapid-Fire Campaign Angenres for Ecommerce Lists
cards.summary: A catalog of niche-agnostic email angles you can bolt onto a calendar when ideas run dry.
cards.use_when: When building monthly calendars and needing more micro-topic campaign angles across the store.

cards.title: Building a Monthly Campaign Calendar
cards.summary: Sequence anchor dates, supplementary sends and micro-topic campaigns into a structured monthly calendar.
cards.use_when: Turning a library of campaign ideas into an actual send schedule for your store.

cards.title: Segmentation: Dynamic Segments vs Static Lists
cards.summary: Understand segments as dynamic, self-updating subsets so you can send the right content to the right slice.
cards.use_when: Designing list architecture in Klaviyo or similar before building campaigns and flows.

cards.title: Email Engagement Segments for Deliverability
cards.summary: Build the core engaged/unengaged suppression sets that protect inbox placement and control sending costs.
cards.use_when: Setting up your base sending architecture so campaigns never blast the full list.

cards.title: Store-Engagement Segments to Find Funnel Leaks
cards.summary: Segment by on-site behavior to spot where buyers drop off and target them directly.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing conversion loss and building targeted campaigns beyond flows.

cards.title: High Potential Purchaser Segment
cards.summary: Create a segment of recent site-active non-buyers to send extra nudges on top of the engaged list.
cards.use_when: Running an extra sale or push to people who are actively shopping but haven't purchased.

cards.title: VIP Segment Built on Purchase Count
cards.summary: Define VIPs by order count rather than spend to make milestones predictable and promotable.
cards.use_when: Designing a loyalty/VIP segment and corresponding email cadence.

cards.title: Winback and Unengaged: Distinguishing Two Recovery Segments
cards.summary: Keep email-unengaged and past-customer winback segments separate because they solve different problems.
cards.use_when: Building reactivation and repurchase campaigns for your list.

cards.title: Predictive Analytics for AOV, CLV and Replenishment Timing
cards.summary: Use Klaviyo predictive analytics to target high spenders, VIPs and near-repurchase groups.
cards.use_when: Upgrading segmentation beyond basic behavior to optimize offers and timing.

cards.title: Location Segmentation for Pop-Ups and Regional Offers
cards.summary: Segment by geography to target local events, region-specific stores and compliance needs.
cards.use_when: Running pop-up shops, in-person events or country-specific storefronts.

cards.title: Cadence and Content Rule: Send Three to Four Emails a Week
cards.summary: High-frequency, high-quality campaigning to engaged segments outperforms low-frequency sending.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many campaigns per week to run and worried about unsubscribes.

cards.title: Build core Klaviyo segments: VIP, winback, suppress, engaged
cards.summary: Four baseline segments (VIP, winback potential, suppress, unengaged) cover most lifecycle revenue without over-segmenting.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing your store's email segmentation and deciding which lists to actually send to and suppress.

cards.title: Interest and cross-sell segments by product/category
cards.summary: Segment by viewed/added/checked-out/purchased product or category to send targeted launches or automated cross-sell flows.
cards.use_when: Planning a product drop, category promo, or automated cross-sell (e.g. buyer of one item toward a complementary item).

cards.title: Resend unopened important emails with the campaign-ID segment trick
cards.summary: Build a 'received X email but didn't open' segment from the campaign message ID, then resend with new subject line and preview text 1-2 days later.
cards.use_when: Maximizing reach on high-value sends like Black Friday, a major product release, or a big announcement.

cards.title: Optimize email copy for the skim, not the read
cards.summary: Assume readers skim in seconds; break copy with line breaks, labels and bold main points so the email is understood in under three seconds.
cards.use_when: Writing or editing any campaign, welcome, or abandoned-cart email where copy currently appears as long paragraphs.

cards.title: Clear and concise email copy: short and sweet, one takeaway
cards.summary: Keep emails to one to two scrolls and one clear takeaway; assume readers are overwhelmed and forget multiple points.
cards.use_when: Writing campaign or flow copy that risks cramming several benefits or messages into one send.

cards.title: Write engaging copy: punchy, informational, entertaining
cards.summary: Trigger dopamine with dense punchy copy, real information, and humor/graphics — repetition kills engagement.
cards.use_when: Writing campaign copy that feels flat, corporate, or repetitive and is underperforming on opens and clicks.

cards.title: Use infographics as email 'secret sauce' to hit all copy principles
cards.summary: Infographics simultaneously make email skimmable, clear/concise and engaging — the source's highest-leverage copy ability.
cards.use_when: Designing email layouts when deciding how to present benefits, comparisons, or product education beyond plain text.

cards.title: Outline email copy in a doc against an existing template
cards.summary: Write copy by physically mapping layout, spacing and sections in a Google Doc modeled on a real email, then hand it to the designer.
cards.use_when: Briefing designers or building any email where you want control over layout placement, not just the words.

cards.title: Prime ChatGPT with your brand, then request punchy hero copy
cards.summary: A two-step ChatGPT prompt — prime with brand/customer context, then request headline, sub-headline and CTA — to get a strong starting draft you edit.
cards.use_when: Facing a blank page on a campaign, drop, or launch email and needing a fast first draft to refine.

cards.title: Prioritize basics before advanced segmentation and copy tricks
cards.summary: Audit whether core flows and popup form conversion are healthy before investing in elaborate segmentation.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to spend limited email/lifecycle effort when the store's fundamentals are still underperforming.

cards.title: Write email copy with an AI prompt + real email outline
cards.summary: Copy a proven competitor email's structure, then use a ChatGPT prompt with brand/customer context to fill the copy.
cards.use_when: You need campaign email copy (best sellers, restock, promo) and want a repeatable fast workflow instead of a blank page.

cards.title: Treat subject lines as frames, and test them on revenue
cards.summary: Subject line and preview text change the psychological frame of the email and can triple sales with identical content, so pick winners by revenue not opens.
cards.use_when: Setting up or interpreting A/B tests on subject lines for any campaign email, especially abandoned cart.

cards.title: Subject line framework: 2–5 words, title case, curiosity loop
cards.summary: Short title-case subject lines that open a curiosity loop and pair with one or two emojis are the source's default format.
cards.use_when: Drafting subject lines for any store campaign — launches, restocks, promos, educational sends.

cards.title: Preview text framework: support the headline, end with an ellipsis
cards.summary: Preview text should be a short supporting line that adds a second curiosity hook, often ending in '...' to prompt the open.
cards.use_when: Writing preview text for any email where the subject line has already been drafted.

cards.title: Build urgency and holidays into seasonal campaign angles
cards.summary: Use real calendar holidays, seasonal timing and scarcity language to give a plain product email a reason to exist.
cards.use_when: Planning a promo or content email with no launch hook — e.g. a nut-bar brand needing a July send.

cards.title: Diagnose and fix weak inbox subject lines
cards.summary: A short review checklist for improving live subject lines: cut length, front-load the hook, and give the preview a job.
cards.use_when: Reviewing your own scheduled campaigns before send, or auditing past sends to improve format.

cards.title: Prioritize content quality and cadence over subject-line tricks
cards.summary: The presenter argues opens should be earned by consistently valuable content and predictable send cadence, with subject lines used only to frame the sale.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much effort to invest in subject-line optimization versus email content and send frequency.

cards.title: Rewrite subject lines as curiosity gap, then judge them by sales
cards.summary: Draft subject line and preview text as a curiosity hook, but validate them on sales/conversion rather than open rate.
cards.use_when: Writing or testing the subject line and preview text for a campaign email, especially a new product or back-in-stock send.

cards.title: Design ecommerce emails in Figma instead of Canva
cards.summary: Use Figma for email design over Canva because layout control and organization hold up better at scale.
cards.use_when: Setting up the design tooling and file structure for a store's recurring email design workflow.

cards.title: Write email copy as a layout brief before design starts
cards.summary: Hand designers a sectioned copy document that shows the intended layout so the design matches the copywriter's intent.
cards.use_when: Briefing an email design (in-house or freelance) for any campaign or flow, to avoid rework between copy and layout.

cards.title: Build a reusable email section template library
cards.summary: Keep pre-built hero, bridge and product section templates in Figma so each new email starts from a proven section.
cards.use_when: Producing email campaigns or flows regularly and wanting to cut design time while keeping section quality consistent.

cards.title: Gradient overlay to place text over a hero image without covering faces
cards.summary: Layer a black-to-transparent gradient rectangle over a hero photo to create readable space for headline, body and CTA.
cards.use_when: Building an email hero where the photo is the background and copy must sit on top of it.

cards.title: Build a CTA button with a rounded rectangle and correct layer order
cards.summary: Construct email CTA buttons as rounded rectangles with text layered on top, and fix z-order when text disappears.
cards.use_when: Creating the primary CTA in an email hero or section where no button template exists.

cards.title: Put the first CTA button above the fold and keep buttons large
cards.summary: Place a large, visible CTA near the top of the email and remove competing nav buttons that dilute clicks.
cards.use_when: Restructuring an underperforming email template, or reviewing an existing template's CTA placement and button sizing.

cards.title: Give every product its own Shop Now button, or at minimum underline the product name
cards.summary: Make clickability obvious on each product tile so the reader can shop a specific item directly from the email.
cards.use_when: Laying out a product grid or multi-product section in a campaign email.

cards.title: Add review counts and short product descriptors to fill out product tiles
cards.summary: Enrich each product tile with rating and a one-line product attribute so the section feels substantial without becoming cluttered.
cards.use_when: Designing or refreshing a multi-product email section that currently looks sparse.

cards.title: Build a visual theme and repeat it across sections for depth
cards.summary: Use gradients and repeated line motifs to make a flat email feel dimensional and cohesive.
cards.use_when: An email section or whole campaign design reads as flat, two-dimensional or off-brand.

cards.title: Use layering and grouping to keep long email files navigable
cards.summary: Group each email section into named frames with inner sub-groups so a long email file stays editable.
cards.use_when: Managing a large email design file that spans multiple sections and will need edits or reuse.

cards.title: Close with a general Shop Now CTA after the product section
cards.summary: End every product section with a broad shop CTA so readers who wanted none of the featured items still have a path.
cards.use_when: Finishing any email that displays a grid or list of specific products.

cards.title: Build a footer with category shopping links plus trust icons
cards.summary: Treat the footer as the one section present in every email and use it for persistent shop-by-category links and social proof badges.
cards.use_when: Designing or revising the standard footer block used across all campaign and flow emails.

cards.title: Vary layout, imagery and copy between sends to prevent subscriber fatigue
cards.summary: Redesign emails so each send looks different in layout, color, theme and copy tone rather than repeating one template.
cards.use_when: Planning an email calendar and choosing which template or layout each campaign will use.

cards.title: Shift CTA copy from 'learn more' to a concrete value proposition
cards.summary: Replace generic learn-more language with the specific thing the customer gets, such as a free trial.
cards.use_when: Rewriting email hero copy and CTA labels for an offer-driven email.

cards.title: Use vertical stacking over side-by-side layouts in email copy
cards.summary: Lay out comparative copy vertically rather than in back-and-forth columns for easier reading in email.
cards.use_when: Building a bridge or comparison section that contrasts the brand against competitors or alternatives.

cards.title: Slice an email design into separate export images, one link each
cards.summary: Cut the finished Figma design into slices per link target and per manageable image size before export.
cards.use_when: Preparing a designed email for uploading into an ESP as a stack of image blocks.

cards.title: Compress exported email images in a batch before uploading
cards.summary: Run all sliced email images through a batch compressor to cut file weight before uploading to the ESP.
cards.use_when: After slicing an email design and before building the campaign in the ESP.

cards.title: Assemble the sliced email in Klaviyo and attach links and alt text
cards.summary: Rebuild the sliced design in the ESP using stacked image blocks, then apply per-image links and fallback alt text.
cards.use_when: Building the actual sendable campaign from exported image slices in Klaviyo or a comparable ESP.

cards.title: Keep site and email visual worlds consistent
cards.summary: Match email design language to the storefront and social channels so the email feels like the same brand.
cards.use_when: Reviewing email templates against the storefront and social presence before a redesign.

cards.title: Redesign browse-abandonment automations to include a top CTA
cards.summary: Fix triggered browse follow-up emails that show products but give no path back to the store.
cards.use_when: Auditing or redesigning a browse-abandonment or recently-viewed automation that fires after a shopper browses a category.

cards.title: Use an interactive mix-and-match block to demonstrate outfit combinations
cards.summary: Show a GIF or rotating block of bestsellers that customers can combine into outfits, then drive to a single shop CTA.
cards.use_when: Building a merchandising email that needs a fresh layout idea for promoting multiple bestsellers together.

cards.title: Use testimonial and social-proof emails to build trust for later purchases
cards.summary: Send review-led emails that accumulate trust even when they don't convert immediately.
cards.use_when: Planning a non-discount campaign slot aimed at warming a list or an audience segment that hasn't purchased.

cards.title: Use value and educational emails that still carry a shop path
cards.summary: Send content-led emails that teach something useful and still route readers toward products in the same send.
cards.use_when: Filling a campaign slot with value content instead of a promotion, especially for an audience that buys gear or apparel.

cards.title: Design emails as image slices, then link buttons in Klaviyo
cards.summary: How to export a Figma email design as slice images, compress them, and rebuild it in Klaviyo with clickable links and alt-ready structure.
cards.use_when: You have approved email creative in Figma and need to ship it through your ESP (Klaviyo) for a campaign or flow.

cards.title: Use a non-discount email strategy: brand, value, social proof
cards.summary: Build a three-email mix of branded, value, and social-proof emails that promote products subtly instead of discounting.
cards.use_when: Planning a campaign calendar or welcome/engagement flow and you want to protect margin rather than default to discount offers.

cards.title: Source email angles from your own Instagram and website
cards.summary: Mine brand Instagram captions, community language, and site blogs to generate email ideas instead of designing from a blank page.
cards.use_when: You need campaign angles for a store and want ideas that feel on-brand and content-driven rather than purely promotional.

cards.title: Pick email layouts from an inspiration bank of proven brands
cards.summary: Reuse layouts and sections from successful brands' emails rather than inventing new structures each time.
cards.use_when: You are laying out a new campaign email and need proven section structures for hero, product, and footer blocks.

cards.title: Educate with a product 'bridge' section to justify the price
cards.summary: Add an educational section that names product features and ties them to customer benefits to give a reason to buy.
cards.use_when: Designing product or launch emails where the hero alone just says 'shop our shoes' without explaining why the product is good.

cards.title: Build product interest with a GIF 'mix and match' section
cards.summary: Create a flipping GIF that pairs tops and bottoms to help customers visualize a full outfit and click through.
cards.use_when: Designing a merch/bestseller email where you want to show multiple product combinations without a wall of static images.

cards.title: Add texture, gradients, and depth so emails don't look flat
cards.summary: Use background texture, gradients, and layering tricks to make branded emails feel immersive rather than blocky.
cards.use_when: Your email sections look like flat white blocks and you want to add life and flow without changing the copy.

cards.title: Reduce thumb stretch: size and place CTAs for mobile taps
cards.summary: Put large, centered CTAs where a phone-holding thumb can easily reach, because small corner buttons hurt clicks.
cards.use_when: Placing buttons in an email hero or product section and deciding size and position for mobile readers.

cards.title: Give a fallback general CTA plus shop-by-collection at the bottom
cards.summary: Add a broad CTA and category links so shoppers who don't want the featured products still have a path to buy.
cards.use_when: An email features specific products or a niche angle (e.g. yoga) and you want it to convert non-targeted subscribers too.

cards.title: Use big aggregate review counts as a trust signal in emails
cards.summary: Surface verified review volume and select testimonials that answer objections to build trust and goodwill.
cards.use_when: Building a social-proof or reviews email, or adding a trust section to a product email.

cards.title: Write blog emails that sell the click and teach on the way
cards.summary: Structure a content email so the reader clicks through to the full post while getting value in the email itself.
cards.use_when: Sending a blog/content email to drive site traffic and downstream purchases.

cards.title: Lay out copy section-by-section before designing
cards.summary: Plan the email's sections and write the copy in a doc first so design and layout follow a clear structure.
cards.use_when: Starting a new campaign email and you want copy organized before touching the design tool.

cards.title: Choose a design tool that supports advanced layout
cards.summary: Prefer a more capable design tool (Figma) over basic tools when building immersive, layered email designs.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to design campaign emails and needing layered type, gradients, background removal, and GIF plugins.

cards.title: Keep the CTA goal singular even with many buttons
cards.summary: A long email can have many buttons as long as they all drive one decision, not several competing ones.
cards.use_when: Designing a multi-section email and deciding how many CTAs to include.

cards.title: Compress email images to protect load time
cards.summary: Compress exported email slice images before upload so the email loads fast in the inbox.
cards.use_when: Preparing Figma slice exports for upload to your ESP.

cards.title: Match email design and copy to the brand's voice
cards.summary: Carry the brand's visual identity, fonts, and tone into email so it doesn't read as generic or corporate.
cards.use_when: An email looks bland/corporate compared to the brand's social presence and you want it to feel on-brand.
